proposal.title: Courts Protect Tenants at 100 Central Park South from Trump’s Demolition Plan
proposal.description_short: A 1998 report said courts protected tenants at 100 Central Park South from Trump’s demolition plan; the building later became Trump Parc East.
proposal.description_medium: On March 26, 1998, The New York Times reported that courts had protected tenants at 100 Central Park South after Donald Trump announced plans to demolish the building. The building remained standing and became Trump Parc East, a condominium; some tenants prepared to buy their apartments while others stayed renters. The report does not substantiate the separate money-laundering allegation about this property or 610 Park Avenue.
proposal.description_long: On March 26, 1998, The New York Times described the end of a dispute between Donald Trump and tenants at 100 Central Park South. The report says Trump had announced plans to tear down the building, while rent-regulated tenants vowed to stay. Courts protected tenants’ rights, and the building remained standing. Trump shifted to converting it into Trump Parc East, a condominium. The story reported that some tenants were preparing to buy their apartments, while others would remain renters. This account supports a specific tenant-rights and development dispute at 100 Central Park South. It does not substantiate the original money-laundering claim, and it gives no evidence about a corresponding event at 610 Park Avenue. The broader two-property allegation should therefore be removed from this item. The New York Times report supplies the event chronology and tenant outcome; it does not describe financial misconduct. This proposal retitles the record around the documented dispute and limits it to the property identified in the report.

proposal.title: NDSU Report Estimates $14.9 Billion Annualized China Tariff Shortfall
proposal.description_short: A May 2026 NDSU report estimates China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs cut U.S. agricultural exports by $14.9 billion annualized.
proposal.description_medium: A May 2026 North Dakota State University report estimates that China’s retaliatory tariffs reduced U.S. agricultural exports to China by $14.9 billion on an annualized basis during March 2025–February 2026. The model assigns about $6.8 billion of the shortfall to soybeans. These are estimates of China-bound exports and a modeled tariff effect, not measured net losses to farmers or a 72% soybean-export collapse.
proposal.description_long: A May 2026 report by North Dakota State University researchers assessed the effects of China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural exports. Using a structural gravity model, the authors estimated an annualized $14.9 billion shortfall in U.S. exports to China over March 2025 through February 2026, relative to a 2024 export baseline. The report attributes the modeled shortfall to China’s Fentanyl and Reciprocal tariff layers and estimates that soybeans account for about $6.8 billion. It also explains that the model separates tariff effects from other influences, including global commodity trends, exporter and importer shocks, seasonality, and monthly aggregate shocks. The figure is an estimate of China-bound export sales, not a direct measure of net harm to U.S. farmers. The report does not support the source record’s claim of a 72% soybean-export collapse. The AgEcon Search record dates the report to May 19, 2026, so this proposal treats the item as report-publication context and corrects the March 4, 2025 record date rather than presenting the later estimate as known on that date.
